title: A Longshot Canadian Wine Region Is Winning Over Skeptical Locals—and the World
summary:
After years of experimentation in Eastern Townships, skilled producers are turning hybrids and finicky Vitis vinifera into electric, elegant bottles.

The post A Longshot Canadian Wine Region Is Winning Over Skeptical Locals—and the World appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
A blizzard was coming, the sky grew dark, and Anne-Marie Lemire was remarkably unbothered.

“It’s been 25 years since we’ve had a storm like this,” said Lemire, the owner of Vignoble Courville in Quebec’s Eastern Townships. I stood in her warmly lit tasting room, peering out the windows, wondering if my boots were fully waterproof. (They weren’t.)

As flurries swirled over her 40 acres, Lemire told me how some winemakers in the region drape their vines in geothermal fabrics and intentionally bury them in the snow to protect them from harsher elements. It’s the sort of homegrown ingenuity that -30°F winters require.

“It’s a good day for vin chaud,” she said, and set a pot of mulled wine to warm on the stovetop. If there’s a better snapshot of the casual attitude and aspirational hardiness of Québécois winemaking, I haven’t found it.

Also known as Cantons de l’Est, the Eastern Townships is a startlingly beautiful wine region an hour or so east of Montreal near the Vermont border. If the name isn’t yet familiar, it’s because commercial viticulture here only began in the 1980s. Like all elder Millennials, it’s experienced seismic changes in those 40-odd years.

Most of the developments are positive. Amid an ever-shifting climate, farming and winemaking practices have evolved and improved. After years of experimentation, skilled producers are now able to turn hybrids and finicky Vitis vinifera into electric, elegant bottles that impress skeptical locals and international critics. You’ll see them on the lists of the coolest wine bars and restaurants in Montreal, not to mention in Toronto, New York, and beyond.

All of this makes for an especially meaningful time for Eastern Townships wine. With fresh momentum and buzzy interest near and far, what happens next feels poignant. Can this patchwork of fiercely independent producers come together to codify their wine scene and compete on a global stage? Do they even want to?

One of the first wineries to showcase the region’s potential was Les Pervenches, a 10-acre, small-production family operation near Farnham. Home to some of the oldest vinifera vines in Quebec, it’s helmed by Véronique Hupin and Mike Marrler, who have been certified organic since 2007 and biodynamic since 2008.

“We’re farmers first,” Hupin said as she poured me a glass of minerally, single-vineyard Chardonnay in her cozy tasting room on a far sunnier day.

I am lucky to try it; Les Pervenches’ vintages almost always sell out immediately. Most bottles go to club members and devoted somms and restaurateurs. In addition to that crisp, linear Chardonnay, their range includes a showstopping Pinot Noir, plus Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Zweigelt, and a blend of Chardonnay with Seyval Blanc, a hybrid white-wine grape bred in Wisconsin to withstand cold temperatures.

Seyval Blanc is one of several hybrid varieties that thrive in the Eastern Townships’ Nordic terroirs and tough winters. Some 80% of all wine grapes planted in Quebec are hybrids, with Frontenac Noir, Frontenac Blanc, and Vidal leading the pack. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are the most common vinifera, but they account for around 6% and 4% of all plantings, respectively.

“Here in Quebec, we used to always drink French and Italian wine, so it’s a big step to drink what is different and what is made here,” Lemire says. “People are accepting more and more that you can make quality wines with hybrids.”

It’s easy to see why. During the last 10 to 15 years, talented Eastern Townships winemakers have transformed the local wine scene. It’s no longer all about what Les Pervenches’ Marler calls “tourist wine,” or treacly bottlings geared toward travelers who primarily think of vineyards as photogenic backdrops for weddings.

Instead, a crop of independent producers has focused on how to ripen vinifera in their short growing season, and how to finesse the searing acidity and distinctive flavors of hybrid grapes. It’s a quality-minded, climate-resistant approach.

“Quebec winemakers are some of the best in the wine industry at managing climate change because we have had to manage a complicated environment since day one,” says Frédéric Simon, co-owner of the boutique winery Pinard et Filles. “For us, it’s not, are we going to get a spring frost? It’s when are we going to get a spring frost?”

I contemplated this existentialistic commitment to preparedness as I stood with Simon on his windswept 18.5 acres. In 2011, he and his co-founder and wife, Catherine Belanger, began sustainably farming the plot off a tree-lined road near Lake Memphremagog. Now in their 10th vintage, they grow some 24 varieties of hybrids and vinifera. Bottlings span an ethereal blanc de blancs, varietal Chardonnay, complex skin-contact wines, and crunchy red blends made with Gamay and Marquette, among others.

With limited production and chic labels designed by Montreal-based artist Marc Séguin, Pinard et Filles has garnered cult status in Quebec and beyond. A handful of bottles are exported to the United States by New York-based importer Zev Rovine Selections. “There’s this incredible amount of extra work it takes to do wine up there,” Rovine says. “It’s inspiring in one way, and head-scratching in another.”

Despite the mounting enthusiasm and recognition for their hard-won expertise, Eastern Townships winemakers still face a slew of misconceptions at home and abroad. “For an American or a European, when they think of Quebec, they think of Eskimos and igloos and winter,” Simon says. “They think that it’s so harsh living here and so cold. When we tell them that we’re making wine here, they’re like, ‘Wait, you make wine? What are you growing? Are you making wine with rhubarbs?’”

Without a rhubarb in sight, what does seem to be gaining ground in the Eastern Townships is sparkling wine production. Wineries like Le Domaine Bergeville in Hatley use hybrids and vinifera, or blends of both, to make complex, traditional-method bubbles.

“There’s unique tension and freshness to these wines,” says Joanie Métivier, the beverage director of Manoir Hovey, a resort in North Hatley. She credits this to winemakers learning how to balance the naturally high acidity of their grapes. “Because we have these very cold winters, people forget that we also have a beautiful growing season with very warm summers.”

Manoir Hovey is a Relais & Chateaux property whose fine-dining restaurant pairs tasting menus with local and world-famous wines, but where it’s also socially acceptable to wear ski pants to breakfast. Tourism here is on the upswing; Métivier has noticed more visitors coming to the Eastern Townships ever since the pandemic.

The local market is evolving, too. As tariffs continue to influence what people eat and drink, many Québécois are appreciative of the bounty in their backyards. “Fifteen years ago, when we started talking about making quality wine in Quebec, it seemed impossible to a lot of people,” Simon says. “Now, more and more people are interested in what we are trying to do.” Within the next decade, Eastern Townships wine “will get the global recognition that it deserves,” he predicts.

In the meantime, there’s an opportunity for area winemakers to define and classify their terroirs, Métivier says. It’s not a bid for increased governmental regulation, like the American Viticultural Area system that delineates Oak Knoll from Stags Leap in the Napa Valley. Instead, it’s an effort to highlight and sustain the momentum that winemakers here have worked so tirelessly to build.

“We’re not trying to make Napa wines or Bordeaux wines,” Métivier says. “We want to make Quebec wines.”

content:
Carl Jung famously theorized that ideas surface simultaneously in unconnected minds, drawn from a shared reservoir he called the collective unconscious. Usually this theory is invoked to explain myths or creative phenomena. Lately it explains something that’s happening in what I’ll call the cocktail unconscious: the great re-awakening of Hpnotiq. You know, the vodka-based neon-blue liqueur popularized by the early 2000s hip-hop scene. 

For the uninitiated: Hpnotiq is a French liqueur made with tropical fruit juices (including mango and passion fruit), vodka, and a touch of cognac. It debuted in 2001, and within three years it went from roughly a thousand cases sold to over a million, thanks to word of mouth, a nightclub stunt involving an Incredible Hulk costume, and the legendary Master P lyric “My favorite drink is that Incredible Hulk (Uuuughhhh!).”

The Incredible Hulk, a lurid green Hennessy-Hpnotiq cocktail sure to give you a good time (and story to tell) became shorthand for a specific era of club culture. I will age myself here and admit that during Hpnotiq’s mid-aughts peak, I was a junior in high school. I should specify: I was a junior in high school in Miami, which means my first Incredible Hulk was purchased with a fake ID at a club. 

My palate couldn’t handle the bitterness of Hennessy back then, but sweet, fruity Hpnotiq was music to my mouth. The glitzy, psychedelic bottle became a must-have showpiece for a boat day. Hpnotiq was even in the room—or rather, the jacuzzi—the day I had sex for the first time. Clearly I have fond memories, and I’m not alone.

Lou Charbonneau, beverage director of Boston-based Xenia Greek Hospitality, smuggled Hpnotiq into his college dorm. “There were definitely Incredible Hulks being made, like, very crudely,” he says. “I should also add that it was a dry campus.” 

Fast forward to 2023, when Charbonneau threw a cyberpunk-themed Halloween party at Hecate, a bar in Boston’s Back Bay neighborhood and part of Xenia, where a regular night in its black-and-gold cave feels like descending into the underworld. For one night Charbonneau turned the space into a futuristic dive bar with neon lights, a frozen machine, and—you guessed it—a Hpnotiq cocktail.

“I wanted a tongue-in-cheek offering, to make it a fever dream for anyone who came in,” he says. “Everyone was so excited for Hpnotiq to be anywhere.” 

Afterward he couldn’t stop thinking about how to fold the liqueur beloved by nightclub-going party animals into Hecate’s high-concept menu, where every cocktail has a mythology and bartenders are “spirit guides.” 

He succeeded with Clarke’s Third Law, a drink containing mellowcorn, freeze-dried fassionola, acidified Pocari Sweat (a Japanese sports drink), powdered albumin (an essential protein found in human blood), and Hpnotiq to round it out. It’s named after Arthur C. Clarke’s notion that any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic. 

While developing the drink for the Hecate party, Charbonneau recalls, “I kept asking what would be accessible and necessary in the future.” 

He landed on water, vitamins, electrolytes, corn, and Hpnotiq—it does have a blend of tropical fruits, after all. The Clarke’s Third Law was a smashing hit.

One mile away, connected in the cocktail unconscious, Eliza Hoar was also putting Hpnotiq on the menu at Equal Measure in Fenway, Boston. She and Charbonneau had been introduced by mutual friend Jay Giordano from the distillery Heaven Hill (the company would soon fold Hpnotiq into its portfolio—synchronicities abound!). 

The happy accident led to a match made in Hpnotiq: they drank it, took uncoordinated but nearly identical photos holding the radioactive-looking bottle in moody lighting at their respective venues, discovered each other’s photos, and joked about collectively championing the liqueur. 

You know what they say: in every joke there’s a spark of truth.

Where’s the Hpnotiq Party At?

Once Giordano started working for Heaven Hill, he did his part to champion it as well. “Jay got his hands on the photos Eliza and I took and shared them on Instagram. Everyone was like, is there a Hpnotiq party happening?” Charbonneau says. 

The response was overwhelming, though a few rolled their eyes. “The majority of bartenders scoff at Hpnotiq, but I don’t think we ought to scoff at anything,” he argues. “If we’re talking lowbrow or detested products, Malört fits in there too.” 

Rather than shy away, Charbonneau is leaning in. He uses Malört, a wormwood liqueur, to give structure and bitterness to Hpnotiq, a combination that has since appeared in his pop-ups nationwide. Bar Vlaha, also part of Xenia, serves Hpnotiq in a guava-and-dill swizzle with Ocho Plata and green Chartreuse. Hecate’s next menu will introduce the Moonchild, with Ocho tequila, lacto-fermented cherry soda, bitter Hpnotiq, and a Maillard chocolate air foam.

Meanwhile Hoar is holding down Hpnotiq on the West Coast. After moving to California to become the director of bars at Rosewood Miramar Beach in May 2025, she has wanted to sneak it onto the hotel’s Manor Bar menu, she says, “but not make an Incredible Hulk.” 

The self-proclaimed geek leaned into a literary theme, pulling from novels, screenplays, and lyrics that romanticize California. Her “California Love” is made with Grey Goose, Hpnotiq, lemon, and sparkling wine, served in a tulip-shaped glass adorned with a crystal bandana. It’s a flip on a French 75, Hoar explains, and an homage to Tupac’s Compton, his favorite drink, and the lyrics “one part Alizé, one part Cristal. Thug’s passion, baby.” 

This year, The Manor Bar joined the 50 Best Discovery List. Hoar is now at work on their next new menu, inspired by spies and meant to read like a case file. There will of course be a Vesper honoring Ian Fleming’s debut Bond novel, Casino Royale, but also, don’t be surprised to spot something Hpnotiq-blue.

A Neon Revolution

The cocktail unconscious continues to churn: At another luxe hotel nearby, Fairmont Breakers Long Beach, bartender Roberto Del Campo is hoping a different neon-colored liqueur gets its day in the sun. Enter the Midori Sour, only available for Monday industry nights at HALO Rooftop Bar. Suntory launched Midori (the Japanese word for green) in the U.S. market in 1978, with an exclusive debut at Studio 54 that coincided with a party for the Saturday Night Fever cast. The sweet liqueur ruled the disco era, only to become regarded as a cheap party trick in elite mixology circles. Its arc from punchline back to prestige remains to be seen. 

Jay Giordano put it best: “Some of [the change] has to do with the industry in general kind of lightening up. When people like Eliza and Lou, who are at the top of their game, play around in this way that’s still elevated, it inspires healthy competition in the younger generation.”

  3. Forget house wines. Restaurants are making their own house spirits too.
  4. Newly available in the U.S., still-strength tequila is taking over.
  5. And soju is experiencing a boom in U.S. markets.

title: Are Reservation-Only Tasting Rooms Hurting Wineries?
summary:
Shifting to reservations helped tasting rooms stay afloat during the pandemic. With visitation down, that may be hurting wineries more than helping.

The post Are Reservation-Only Tasting Rooms Hurting Wineries? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Mandatory pandemic restrictions forced California wineries to switch to reservation systems, but post-lockdown demand has since fallen to 20-year lows.
  • Consumers miss spontaneous walk-ins, prompting many wineries to adopt flexible, hybrid models to boost foot traffic and sales.
  • Reservations enable personalized guest experiences, though local permit restrictions often dictate whether walk-ins are legally allowed.

In the early aughts, most California wineries operated on a drop-in basis. Guests could roll up to their favorite winery, sip through a line-up, enjoy the views, and then move on. 

When Covid-19 hit, that model fell out of favor for practical reasons, and wineries relied more on reservations to welcome in guests. These measures were helpful in facilitating social distancing and safer visitations. However, as restrictions were lifted, the reservation system stuck. 

Many winery teams argue that reservations create more intimate, customized experiences, while helping them save on staffing costs. But some consumers argue that, when tasting rooms require reservations, visiting them feels less welcoming, and removes any chance of spontaneity.

This debate is amplified by the fact that tasting room visits at U.S. wineries have not returned to pre-pandemic numbers. Demand has slumped, hitting a 20-year low.

As a result, some wineries are switching approaches. “You’re seeing a lot of sandwich boards in Napa Valley that say, we accept walk-ins,” says Vida DeLong, who runs Hopscotch DTC consulting.

So, what’s the right reservation model?

A Post-Covid Shake-Up

When businesses reopened after Covid-19 shutdowns, operators realized the reservation model came with myriad benefits. “It allowed better planning, an understanding of what was coming up,” says Jonathan Wendorf, director of consumer sales and marketing at Sequoia Grove Winery.

As post-lockdown tourism rebounded, sales were strong—until they weren’t. When, ostensibly, the excitement of getting back to wine country wore off, businesses began to scramble. “People are looking to take walk-ins—do everything that they can,” Wendorf says.

California’s J. Lohr Vineyards has switched from a reservations-only model to a reservations-encouraged model. “With traffic being down and guests expecting walk-in service again, we are able to accommodate both,” says Jessica Kolhoff, director of hospitality and direct sales. 

Sure, they have to be more reactive with staffing, entertaining a growing number of “custom” guest experiences. “There is an expectation for seated tastings, indoor versus outdoor options,  food, and special accommodations—kids, large parties, lingering visits, etc.,” says Kollhoff. “The expectation around the level of hospitality is also higher.”

With growing inflation and ever-rising tasting fees, can we blame consumers?

“With the increased fees associated with tastings valley-wide, tourists are, rightfully, expecting a more elevated experience than those that Napa was known for in its earlier days,” says Luke Jeramaz, digital marketing manager at Grgich Hills Estate. “They expect a degree of privacy, a peaceful setting, and a knowledgeable host that personalizes their experience.”

Grgich still embraces both reservations and walk-ins, but the split has changed. Pre-pandemic, 70% of guests were walk-in only. Now, 85% of guests book ahead of time. 

With its inherent need for more staff, this business model is no easy feat to maintain, but it does work. “Our wine educators maintain steady work hours, and our guests receive far more personalized, one-on-one experiences,” says Jeramaz. “The added expense is balanced out by the fact that we rarely have to turn away guests, leading to greater tasting room traffic and increased chances of conversions.”

Weighing What Customers Want 

DeLong has found the hybrid model is working well for her clients, primarily because what visitors want from the region has changed. 

“What we’re finding is that visitors [and] day-trippers want to just play it by ear and see where the day takes them,” she says. 

Many wineries have launched urban tasting rooms, capturing travelers who don’t want to spend an hour driving and finding parking in wine country, and for whom a $180, two-hour tasting doesn’t appeal. “They don’t need to drive, and they can hit six, seven, eight different tasting rooms in an afternoon with zero planning,” DeLong explains.

There’s also the saturation factor—Napa Valley has a large number of wineries to choose from (around 475, though not all offer tastings).

“There are too many tasting options for the number of visitors,” says DeLong. “If you’re a visitor, there’s an economic consideration and limited time.” 

Then, there’s the lack of spontaneity. “If you’re driving down one of the corridors and something catches your eye, the opportunity to pull over is great,” says Wendorf. “That’s half the fun of exploring.”

While he finds that people who make reservations tend to be more engaged with the brand—it’s that specific winery they wanted to spend their day and money—there are benefits to both camps. “On the other hand, the walk-in consumer is fun because you don’t know who they are,” Wendorf explains. It could be a buyer with interest, a big spender with time, or someone who could be a future fan. 

“You get to create a new brand ambassador—somebody who falls in love with what they experience,” he says. “The walk-in gives you a bigger opportunity for club conversions because they have no expectations. You can wow them. It’s a clean slate moment. Or, you can turn them off. If they walk in and you turn them away, even if the winery is empty, it’s a relationship lost.”

In Defense of Reservations

This isn’t to say a tasting room reservations system is a full-stop bad idea.

Sarah Citron, CEO of Bricoleur Vineyards, operates on a 90% reservation-based model. It allows the staff to curate every experience and ensures the kitchen is stocked and the hospitality team knows who’s coming. 

“Walk-ins add a beautiful spontaneity, but without the reservation infrastructure, it would be difficult to deliver the level of hospitality we’re committed to,” says Citron. “Reservations make the elevated experience financially and operationally sustainable, and attract that audience because it signals that what we offer is worth planning for.” 

Ehlers Estate is reservation-only, based on its permit, but that hasn’t proved to be an issue, according to director of sales and marketing Sandra DeMaria.  She finds that her guests are planners: 45% of people make reservations at least two weeks in advance. First time buyers, on average, make reservations at least three to five weeks in advance. Forty percent of guests are club members.

“They’re really planning way ahead before they come to the valley,” DeMaria says. “It has given us the opportunity to create experiences and have a connection before people come.” This approach has proved successful for Ehlers: On average, guests spend between $125 and $175 per visit, and usually purchase at least three bottles. 

For some consumers, planning detailed itineraries far in advance helps make the most of their travel investment. Visitors from Los Angeles spend, on average, nearly $4,000 per trip, according to Visit Napa Valley. If people are going to spend the money to come to Napa, stay overnight, and book the nanny, they want confirmed fun. 

Not all reservations are the same, staid, flight-and-lecture experience, either. Shadybrook Estate Winery tours guests around on horseback. Tank Garage hosts themed tasting events, including Italian Disco deejay sets and arcade parties. Ehlers Estate offers a Traitors-esque game played at communal tables where guests can interact.

What works for each winery depends on what their consumer wants. 

DeLong encourages her team to pivot if certain experiences aren’t selling or guests don’t seem engaged. “There will always be demand for incredible, bespoke, luxury-oriented, cerebral, high-touch experiences,” she says. “Those will always be popular with certain visitors. But the wineries who are able to be flexible, nimble, and curious while staying loyal to their brand ethos are the ones that are winning.”

Valley Rules

Due to rules and regulations of local ordinances, not every winery can welcome walk-ins. Daily and annual visitation limits are also dictated by county permits.

“The primary reason we are by reservation-only is due to our permit restrictions,” says Florencia Palmaz, CEO of Palmaz Vineyards. “We were never allowed to explore a different option of tour and tasting formats.” 

But it’s not a burden, Palmaz says. She finds that her team can forge closer relationships with their customers as a result. 

“Offering private tours allows each visitor to really explore the areas of wine that interest them,” she notes. “If a guest is interested in technology, then we will tailor the visit to their interest. If a guest is coming back for a second time, we are happy to pivot to a different area of winemaking or winegrowing.”

Citron agrees. “Today’s wine tourist wants meaning, not just wine. They’re looking for connection to the land, to the people making the wine, and to each other.”

title: This Low-ABV Breakfast Spritz Tastes Like the Amalfi Coast
summary:
The refreshing low-proof Breakfast Spritz served at Casa Angelina in Praiano, Italy, is made with tea, Sherry, lemon, and honey.

The post This Low-ABV Breakfast Spritz Tastes Like the Amalfi Coast appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Perhaps it was only a matter of time before spritzes conquered breakfast. 

The Breakfast Spritz, an herbal, slightly sweet cocktail garnished with local honeycomb, is one of the most popular cocktails served at Casa Angelina, a luxe hotel located in the cliffs of Praiano on the Amalfi Coast. Made with English breakfast tea, Sherry, honey, and fresh lemon, the spritz is refreshing, earthy, and invigorating all at once, with an even lower abv than your standard spritz.

“Our classic cocktails are still very popular, but we’ve seen more and more guests showing interest in lower-alcohol drinks,” says bartender Marco Giordano, who developed the recipe for the hotel’s Seascape Bar. Overlooking the Tyrrhenian Sea, with views of Positano and Capri framed by oversized windows, the elegant all-white bar offers guests a dedicated spritz menu, which includes a section for lower-alcohol options, as well as Champagne spritzes and an array of Italian riffs. 

“Tea, honey, and lemon are all typical breakfast flavors, and we wanted to reinterpret them in a light, refreshing cocktail,” says Giordano. This year, the property introduced beehives into its cliffside garden, which supplies the honey for the drink. In fact, most of the ingredients for the cocktails at Seascape Bar are sourced from its steep garden, which climbs almost vertically to the sky and also provides the hotel with tomatoes, herbs, eggs, and seasonal produce. 

Despite its name, guests mostly order the cocktail in the afternoon. “It’s actually most popular by the pool,” says Giordano. “Guests usually order it during the afternoon while relaxing in the sun. It’s light, refreshing, and easy to drink, which makes it perfect for the Amalfi Coast climate.”

The Breakfast Spritz

From bartender Marco Giordano

Ingredients

⅓ ounce Sherry
2 ⅓ ounces of English Breakfast tea
⅓ ounce honey
⅓ ounce fresh lemon juice
2 ounces soda water
Optional garnishes: fresh mint, honeycomb, Maraschino cherry

Instructions

  1. Dissolve the honey in the fresh lemon juice. 
  2. Pour into a large wine glass, add the Sherry and chilled English Breakfast tea, then stir gently. 
  3. Fill the glass with ice and top with soda water. Garnish with a small piece of honeycomb, a cherry, and a sprig of fresh mint.

title: The Best Wines for Every Zodiac Sign
summary:
Should we be looking to the stars when picking a wine?

The post The Best Wines for Every Zodiac Sign appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Love it or think it’s ridiculous, astrology has increasingly worked its way into popular culture and the general psyche.

Major magazines, from Cosmopolitan and Elle to Vogue and GQ, regularly cover the topic, publishing horoscopes and articles about how the planets are impacting various aspects of life. Social media is full of astrological influencers. Pop artists, like Kacey Musgraves, SZA, and Ariana Grande, have sung about Saturn and its return in their music.

According to a survey of 2,000 young Americans, around 80% of all Gen Z and millennials believe in astrology—a significant portion of whom use the practice to make career and other major life decisions.

This got us wondering: Should we be looking to the stars when picking a wine, too?

Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large Tonya Pitts thinks so.

“I am a firm believer that everything is connected and people gravitate to people, places, and things that spark something inside them; it could be joy, passion, intrigue, or memories from the past,” she says. “There are those that say it has nothing to do with anything, but I like to think it’s all in the stars and planetary alignments.”

To help guide the various zodiac signs toward specific wine that may resonate with their various attributes, Pitts took into account the general flavor profiles of grape varietals and along with regional attributes. Then, she sought out bottles that evoke emotion and translate into traits of behaviors of the signs, essentially thinking if a varietal were a person, what would it taste like and what sort of emotions would it produce?

“It’s no simple formula,” she adds. While she did her best to map it all out, Pitts admits, “every prediction or thought doesn’t line up with everyone either.”

So, what, precisely, are her astrological wine picks? Check them out below.

Aries (March 21 – April 19): Syrah

Themes: “Bold and ambitious, Aries dives headfirst into even the most challenging situations—and they’ll make sure they always come out on top,” says Pitts.

Why: “Syrah is bold and ambitious, like an Aries. Often a sleeper hit, it’s a wine that always strives to stand out, much like those born under this sign. Syrah is grown around the globe. It is always fantastic and intriguing, much like the ram.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Pursued by Bear 2022 Baby Bear Syrah (Columbia Valley (WA))

Baby Bear is a perfect name for this Syrah, as I consider it a “Goldilock’s wine” where everything is just right. The first aroma to catch your attention is pure blackberry pie. The fruit is followed by puffs of mint and pork chops roasting over a salty driftwood fire at the beach. Black cherry and espresso flavors are joined by the tiniest bit of anise. This Baby Bear hibernated for 30 months in 17% new and 83% used 600L puncheons. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — Michael Alberty

$58 Wine.com

Château de Nages 2021 JT Syrah (Costières de Nîmes)

Composed of 95% Syrah and 5% Mourvèdre, this wine opens with blackberry and kirsch compote, dried thyme, violets, black peppercorn and earthy depth on the nose. Energetic and juicy, it delivers ample blackberry fruit with an edge of white pepper. Silky yet powerful, it finishes long making it a good companion for layered dishes such as moussaka. 92 Points — Anna-Christina Cabrales

$30 Total Wine & More

Taurus (April 20 – May 20): Mourvèdre

Themes: “Tauruses are oriented around the physical world,” says Pitts. “Bulls tend to be grounded and logical. They love routine and they’re committed to their own comfort.”

Why: “Mourvèdre is a grounded and supple wine, mirroring Taurus’s love for routine and comfort. Known for its floral notes and dark fruit flavors like blackberry and boysenberry, Mourvèdre is both forceful and subtle, making it a perfect match for the grounded nature of a Taurus.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Stiekema 2024 Mourvèdre (Paso Robles)

This blend of Calesta and Kiler Canyon vineyards is a lavish and detailed style of Mourvèdre, starting with dark cherry and woodspice aromas on the nose. The palate is bold and expressive, offering blackberry, dark cherry, nutmeg, and woodspice flavors. 94 Points — Matt Kettmann

$54 Stiekema

Miraflores Winery 2023 Estate Mourvèdre (El Dorado County)

Aromatic with notes of wild black strawberries, raspberries, dried rose petals, coriander, grilled orange zest, and French oak on the nose; the palate is bright mulberries, dark plums, cassis, pink grapefruit, dried chicory and supple tannins to finish. 93 Points — Tonya Pitts

$38 Miraflores Winery

Gemini (May 21 – June 20): Riesling

Themes: “Spontaneous, playful, and adorably erratic, Geminis are driven by their insatiable curiosity,” says Pitts. “Appropriately symbolized by the celestial twins, this air sign is interested in so many pursuits that it had to double itself.”

Why: “Just like Gemini, Riesling has many faces (and no, that’s not a bad thing). Whether it’s dry or rich with residual sugar, Riesling embodies the duality and versatility of a Gemini, making it an exciting and unpredictable choice that can vary widely depending on where it’s grown.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Fess Parker 2024 Rodney’s Vineyard Riesling (Santa Barbara County)

Classic petrol aromas are cut by lemon sorbet and coconut flake on the nose of this bottling. The palate is racy and texture, pairing brisk Meyer lemon peel flavors with tangerine sorbet and more petrol touches. This should last long. Drink now-2044. Cellar Selection. 94 Points — M.K.

$25 Solano Cellars

Weingut Karl Erbes 2023 Üziger Würzgarten Auslese Riesling (Mosel)

Layered and expressive, with orange blossom, ripe peach, quince, and a hint of tropical fruit forming a generous core. Floral notes and gentle spice add nuance throughout. The sweetness is well-balanced by lively acidity, giving the wine lift and precision. Slightly more restrained in intensity, it still delivers a long, complex finish with elegant persistence. 92 Points — Aleks Zecevic

$35 Plum Market

Cancer (June 21 – July 22): Cabernet Franc

Themes: “Nurturing and loyal, Cancers are also protective of their loved ones,” says Pitts. “They are highly sensitive, deeply caring, and feel everything deeply.”

Why: “Cabernet Franc is nurturing and needs careful attention, just like a Cancer. Depending on how it’s grown, it can range from herbaceous and red-fruited to deep, dark and brooding, reflecting the crab’s depth of emotion and sensitivity.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Domaine de la Petite Roche 2022 Cabernet Franc (Anjou)

This is a gorgeous wine. Perfumed aromas of raspberry-blossom, rosehip, dried-cherry flakes and violet open on the nose followed by black olive and boysenberry. Supple tannins guide a well-integrated mix of red-and-black fruit along a roller-coaster ride of flavors that are showered in pencil shavings, forest floor and dried hay. Best Buy. 92 Points — Reggie Solomon

$19 Union Square Wines & Spirits

Darcie Kent Vineyards 2023 Lemmons Vineyard Cabernet Franc (San Francisco Bay-Livermore Valley)

Livermore Valley has a treasure trove of Cabernet Franc offerings. stylistically, there is an expression that pleases everyone’s palate; this one is concentrated on the nose, with aromas of bramble black currant, black plum, coriander, cedar, and sagebrush. The flavors on the palate are ripe, red plum, cassis, dark cherry, bittersweet chocolate, star anise, and supple tannins on the finish. 92 Points — T.P.

$55 Darcie Kent Vineyards

Leo (July 23 – August 22): Cabernet Sauvignon

Themes: “Passionate, loyal, and infamously dramatic, Leo is represented by the lion and these spirited fire signs are the kings and queens of the celestial jungle,” says Pitts.

Why: “Cabernet Sauvignon is often seen as the king of wines, much like Leo’s place in the zodiac. Known for its boldness and stature in the wine world, the varietal commands attention and is a top choice for a sign that loves to be in the spotlight.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Le Roi 2024 Le Roi Rouge Cabernet Sauvignon Cabernet Sauvignon (Pays d’Oc)

This would be a superb wine at three times the price, offering far more in flavor, texture and stability than most anything in its price class. Deep aromas of blackberry, peppercorn, woodspice and oregano lead from the nose into a rich palate that’s lush but bone dry. Flavors of blue and red fruit are dusted in espresso and baking spice, finishing on a chocolate note. Best Buy. 94 Points — M.K.

$17 Taylor’s Wine Shop

Merriam Vineyards 2021 Gloeckner-Turner Ranch Cabernet Sauvignon (Rockpile)

This dark and rich Cabernet displays intense aromas of reduced berries, plum compote, violets and ginger on the nose. The palate is plush and velvety, with long, smooth tannin, juicy acidity and flavors of raspberry gastrique, blueberry jam, black pepper and herbal potpourri that dances along the finish. Gorgeous now, this will benefit from some time in the cellar. Best 2030-2050. Cellar Selection. 95 Points — Tom R. Capo

$88 Merriam Vineyards

Virgo (August 23 – September 22): Grüner Veltliner

Themes: “Virgos are said to be the most analytical and organized members of the zodiac, as foxes are logical, practical, and systematic in their approach to life,” says Pitts.

Why: “Grüner Veltliner is complex and layered, much like a Virgo. Its pleasing and intricate flavors require attention to detail, making it the ideal wine for this meticulous and practical sign.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Anarchist Wine Co. 2023 The Anarchist Grüner Veltliner (Mokelumne River)

This expression has tossed out the rule about perception and has embraced a what and where I can fit into your daily routine, whether food-wise or kicking back. We are here for it! The aromatics are bright and rich, with a concentration of White nectarine, peach, baked apples, and honeysuckle. At the same time, the palate gallops into White grapefruit, tangerine, turmeric, lifted acidity, and a mouth-watering finish. 92 Points — T.P.

$26 Anarchist Wine Co.

Nittnaus 2022 Elektra Grüner Veltliner (Weinland Österreich)

Exceptionally complex and layered, this wine unfolds with white raspberry, yellow apple, and delicate quince blossom. Vibrant kumquat-like acidity adds tension, while a subtle bitter-sweet undertone enhances the depth. Silky texture, multilayered flavors, and a persistent, long finish make this a truly captivating expression. 94 Points — A.Z.

$20 Union Square Wines & Spirits

Libra (September 23 – October 22): Sauvignon Blanc

Themes: “Libras are known for the love of being around other people. They are a fun and loving extroverted sign,” says Pitts.

Why: “Sauvignon Blanc is a bright and lively wine that makes you want to bask in the sun, just like these swans love being in the company of others. Its fresh and approachable nature reflects Libras’ love of socializing and fun.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Domaine Roc de l’Abbaye 2024 Sauvignon Blanc (Sancerre)

This wine has a flowery, complex nose that draws you in with muddled green pear and keeps you there with aromas of dried hay and lemon blossom. The stony palate boasts vibrant minerality that is in sync with Gala apple on the lengthy palate. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — R.S.

$39 Wine.com

Jules Taylor 2025 Sauvignon Blanc (Marlborough)

This vintage of veteran winemaker Jules Taylor’s classic SB is singing. Bright and bouncy, with passionfruit, lemon-lime, pink grapefruit, fresh tarragon, and basil aromas. The palate is zippy and fresh, a shooting star of acidity amidst an intriguing creamy-pithy texture combo, with a wild edge to the long herb-flecked citrus finish that makes the mouth water for more. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Christina Pickard

$20 Wine.com

Scorpio (October 23 – November 21): Pinot Noir

Themes: “Elusive and mysterious, Scorpio is one of the most misunderstood signs of the zodiac,” says Pitts. “Scorpions are known for their loyalty and devotion—and also their passion.”

Why: “Pinot Noir is often misunderstood, just like Scorpio. It’s a delicate, thin-skinned grape that requires nurturing, but when treated with care, it can be deeply rewarding. Its reputation for being dark and complex mirrors Scorpio’s passionate and enigmatic nature.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Bob Cabral Wines 2022 Cuvée Electric Hippy Pinot Noir (Sonoma Coast)

Explosive aromas of pomegranate molasses, cranberry compote, Darjeeling, nori and roses burst from the glass on the nose of this enticing Pinot. The palate delivers flavors of concentrated Bing cherry, licorice, cinnamon and orange peel in a framework of powder-fine tannin and voluptuous acidity. Brilliant now, this will benefit from some time in the cellar. Best from 2030-2040. Editors’ Choice. 97 Points — T.R.C.

$125 Bob Cabral Wines

Bader-Mimeur 2022 Château de Chassagne-Montrachet Pinot Noir (Chassagne-Montrachet)

This wine feels like the moment after a lover’s quarrel, powerful, seductive and impossible to ignore. The nose is heady with rose petal, iodine, charred meat, black peppercorn, violet, white pepper and fine herbs. Silky on the palate, it carries floral spice and white tea through a long finish. Delicious now, or cellar through 2035. 93 Points — A.C.C.

$56 Wine.com

Sagittarius (November 22 – December 21): Grenache

Themes: “What makes Sagittarius so unique is its dynamic blend of passion, curiosity, intensity, and adaptability,” says Pitts. “The centaur values independence and the ability to do what they want, when they want, above all else.”

Why: “Grenache is versatile and adaptable, much like a Sagittarius. It can stand on its own but also blends well with others, reflecting Sagittarius’s independent yet social nature. Grenache is a perfect match for this adventurous and passionate sign.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

La Lomita Wines 2023 Islay Hill Vineyard Grenache (Edna Valley)

Lavish aromas of boysenberry, raspberry sorbet and alluring baking spice show on the layered, complex and exciting nose of this bottling from an estate that sits on one of the appellation’s volcanic plugs. That strawberry and cherry core is awash in French toast spices, loving rich and bold yet still fresh. 97 Points — M.K.

$68 La Lomita

Capricorn (December 22 – January 19): Aglianico

Themes: “Capricorns are known to be extremely hardworking visionaries, leaders, and trailblazers,” says Pitts. “Pragmatic and proud, sea goats want to be praised both for the reasonable actions they take and their approach to life.”

Why: “Aglianico is a grape that matures into something truly special. Grown in mountainous regions, it starts off with iron-rich, dry red fruit flavors and develops into a solid, earthy wine that leaves a lasting impression, embodying the determination and visionary spirit of a Capricorn.”

Explore more great wines for Capricorns here.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Fontanavecchia 2019 Vigna Cataratte Riserva Aglianico (Aglianico del Taburno)

The nose opens with the warm spiciness of terracotta, oregano and sun-dried tomato, then sweetens with ripe berries layered with salted dark chocolate. The palate is tangy with pomegranate and black plum, before more herbs and bitter chocolate recall the nose. Tannins are decisive but not aggressive, and allow a cooling, minty salinity to play out on the finish. A flex from Fontanavecchia, as this wine undeniably overdelivers. 94 Points — Danielle Callegari

$44 Wine Watch

Monte Volpe 2020 Aglianico (Mendocino County)

The spectrum of Italian varietals grown in California is astounding and plentiful. This one is showing up more often, and it is Aglianico. Unlike its version grown in Italy, the fruit is rich, vibrant dark berries with a softer tannin structure and much more ready to drink even with fuller tannins. It is an absolute match for hearty meals like grilled and roasted meat dishes. 93 Points — Tonya Pitts

$40 Graziano Family Of Wines

Aquarius (January 20 – February 18): Viognier

Themes: “Aquarians are clever, analytical, technical, truthful, assertive, confident, progressive, and innovative,” says Pitts. “These water bearers like to solve problems, improve what’s already working well and push boundaries.” 

Why: “Viognier is a thoughtful and complex wine that, when done right, can be very thought-provoking, just like an Aquarius. Whether blended with Syrah to add a floral touch or enjoyed on its own, Viognier’s ability to stand out reflects Aquarius’s innovative spirit.”

Explore more wines for Aquarians here.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Yalumba 2023 The Virgilius Viognier (Eden Valley)

An oh-so-Viognier perfume lures the senses with heady notes of honeysuckle, cherry blossom, a white peach, lemon curd and white pepper. One you manage to pry your nostrils from the glass to take a sip, you’re met with a fulsome, mouth-filling palate that’s creamy but never heavy or syrupy, those floral and fruit notes flowing more subtly to the finish. Pair with buttered chicken or a Thai curry. 94 Points — C.P.

$50 Wine.come

Cedarville Vineyard 2023 Estate Viognier (El Dorado)

The aromas are lush, with notes of citrus rind, Meyer lemon, Yellow apple, and honeysuckle, layered with honeycomb on the nose. The flavors are marzipan, White nectarine, youthful apple, and lime curd, laced with bright acidity, and a long, mouth-watering finish. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — T.P.

$33 Cedarville Vineyard

Pisces (February 19 – March 20): Chardonnay

Themes: “Pisces is the most intuitive, sensitive, and empathetic sign of the entire zodiac and they will go to great lengths to ensure the happiness of those around them,” says Pitts.

Why: “Chardonnay is a versatile and crowd-pleasing wine, much like the fish. Chardonnay can adapt to different environments, in different regions around the globe. Chardonnay grown in Mendocino Ridge must adapt to the long cold breezes from the nearby ocean, while its counterpart in Livermore Valley gets to bask in the sunshine and enjoy a warm growing season. These regions create completely unique styles of Chardonnay, yet it can please a wide audience, embodying Pisces’s empathetic and caring nature.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

William Fèvre 2023 Vaillons Premier Cru Chardonnay (Chablis)

Crushed stone and green apple mingle on the nose that rests against a wall of baby’s breath and muddled white blossom. The steely palate accentuates purity of fruit while elevating freshness on the finish that is lifted by a nervy layer of acidity. 94 Points — A.C.C.

$93 Wine.com

Presqu’ile Winery 2023 Chardonnay (Santa Maria Valley)

Honeysuckle, lemon-glazed apple and gardenia aromas are very comforting and inviting on the nose of this bottling. There’s a tense landing to the palate, where lemon, lime zest and green apple flavors make for an electric, acid-powered sip. 93 Points — M.K.

title: The 8 Most Iconic Cheese Shops in America
summary:
Curious how to tell the difference between a good and great cheese shop? Consider this guide to retailers from New York to Washington State.

The post The 8 Most Iconic Cheese Shops in America appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
There are several ways to determine what makes a cheese shop worth a visit. And as with many things in food and wine, there aren’t simple answers. But, some guidelines can help you find the best cheese shop for your needs.

Cheese educator David Asher believes how a shop engages with its community is paramount. “A great cheese shop makes connections between the cheese producers and consumers and tries to form a relationship between them,” he says.

This connection is part of a larger cultural shift to understand where and how our foods are made. “Cheese stores can act as a liaison between good farmers producing good cheese and their consumers,” he adds.

Additionally, cheese scholar Carlos Yescas says the difference between a good and a great cheese shop often comes down to what’s for sale and how it’s being sold. A retailer worth its salt will seek out products from cheesemakers that share its values. This could mean supporting independent local producers, sourcing rare international labels, and hiring and training staff to become cheese experts. In doing so, these shops become community hubs of cheese exploration.

You’ll know a good cheesemonger when you meet them because they’ll be excited to talk to you about their products and to cut samples for you to taste, says Christine Clark, a writer and cheese educator.

Willingness to give samples is key, she adds. One person’s cheese preference may be different than another’s. Plus, cheese is a living product and can taste different each time you try it. “Whereas wine has vintages by year, in cheese, each day can be like a new vintage,” Clark says.

If you’re ready to explore the evolving world of artisanal cheese, consider visiting one of these eight iconic cheese shops. While they’re certainly not the only destinations for quality cheese in the United States, this list is a great place to start.

Antonelli’s

Austin, Texas

Opened by husband-wife duo John and Kendall Antonelli in 2010, Antonelli’s has grown into a Hyde Park institution with dozens of cheeses cut to order. Plus, you can find charcuterie, pickles, breads, and other sundries. The brightly lit cafe offers custom boards and gift baskets, and its educational program includes everything from Cheese 101 classes to guided tastings featuring pairings such as charcuterie or halloween candy.

Yescas notes that many Austin chefs source ingredients from Antonelli’s and credits the shop with bringing artisanal cheese culture to a new corner of the country. “They’re a catalyst in their state for better cheese,” he says.

Artisan Cheese Company

Sarasota, Florida

One of Clark’s favorite shops, Artisan Cheese Company, opened a small storefront in 2012 and relocated to its current 2,000-square-foot space in Sarasota’s Rosemary District in 2018. Its expansive selection includes such all-American standard-bearers as Jasper Hill and Point Reyes, as well as hard-to-source European producers like Switzerland’s Gourmino and England’s Neal’s Yard. The airy, industrial digs also feature beer, natural wine, salumi, and more, and the café serves grilled cheese, crostini, and other small plates.

Beecher’s Handmade Cheese

Seattle, Washington

While the Pike’s Place location of this Seattle landmark is admittedly thronged with tourists, Beecher’s earns its spot for longevity and influence. The original glass-walled shop opened in 2003 with a then-uncommon commitment to sourcing milk from local cows not fed recombinant bovine growth hormones and hand-making cheese onsite. Today, the original location has since spawned four cafés throughout Washington and several airport outposts worth a visit.

Fairfield Cheese Company

Fairfield, Connecticut

One of Yescas’ top shops is this storefront with “amazing service” and an extensive selection of small-production U.S. and international cheeses. Fairfield stocks cheeses like Jasper Hill Farms’ ultra-seasonal, spruce-wrapped Winnimere cheese, Amsterdammer Betty Koster’s Brabander Reserve, and more.

“The owners are committed to diversity and inclusion in their mongering, and they’re also doing the hard work of connecting cheese enthusiasts to cheese with their tours,” says Yescas. Fairfield Cheese Company offers classes devoted to U.S., French, and other regional cheeses, and hosts trips to explore far-flung cheese cultures, like sojourns to the United Kingdom, called A British Cheese Odyssey.

Formaggio Kitchen

Cambridge, Massachusetts

“People don’t think Boston is a cheese town, but Boston is one of the original cheese towns. Vermont is our local farm,” says Yescas. He hails Formaggio Kitchen as a standard-bearer in the U.S. artisanal cheese movement, noting how the 1978 Cambridge shop not only served as its own importer of then-hard-to-find European cheeses, but also spawned two other Formaggios in the Boston area and one in New York City. In nearly 50 years of operation, Formaggio has introduced generations of northeasterners to specialty cheeses like Valençay frais (the Loire’s ash-coated goat cheese) and Vermont’s esteemed Jasper Hills.

Fromagination

Madison, Wisconsin

Nearly 50% of U.S. specialty cheeses are made in Wisconsin, and dairy is a point of pride for many in the state. Fromagination on Madison’s Capitol Hill celebrates the local bounty with an extensive collection of Wisconsin labels including Uplands Cheese and Bleu Mont Dairy, plus national and international selections like Norwegian Gjetost and Germany’s crowd-pleasing blue cheese, Cambozola.

Milkfarm

Los Angeles, California

Natural wine and high-end pantry items, like Jacobsen sea salt, line the walls of this well-stocked shop in Los Angeles’ Eagle Rock neighborhood. One of Asher’s favorites, Milkfarm specializes in cheeses from small and independent producers primarily in the L.A. area. It also offers made-to-order sandwiches—including a cult grilled cheese—plus baked goods and cheese boards to enjoy at the counter or sunny sidewalk seating.

Saxelby Cheesemongers

New York, New York

When legendary cheesemaker, educator, and author Anne Saxelby opened Saxelby Cheesemongers in Manhattan’s Chelsea Market in 2006, it was hailed as New York City’s first store dedicated to American-made farmstead and artisanal cheese. Asher and Clark are among the many cheese pros who still sing its praises, citing its friendly atmosphere and knowledgeable cheesemongers who happily cut samples and talk through options with curious customers.

Honorable Mentions

As valuable as cheese shops can be, they aren’t the only places to find great cheese.

“Consider shopping for cheese at a local farmers market, where some of the best small cheese producers sell their stuff,” says Asher. “Some makers, for example, my favorite natural cheesemaker in America, Bobolink Dairy, sell exclusively at NYC-area farmers’ markets.”

Additionally, specialty grocers like Rainbow Grocery in San Francisco and Philadelphia’s Di Bruno Bros. have destination-worthy cheese selections among other gourmet goods.
